title: Return NA for malformed period strings; fix P2H30M meaning months
description:
**Behaviour change.** These malformed strings returned a silent value; they now return `NA`, as `"1X"` already does:

| input | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `".h"` | 0 | NA |
| `"PTM"` | 1 minute | NA |
| `"P1D1D"` | 2 days | NA |
| `"T1H"` | 1 hour | NA |
| `"P1DT"` | 1 day | NA |
| `"1h (2h (3h) 4h) 5h"` | 10 hours | NA |

The rules: a `.` needs a digit on one side. After an ISO `P`, a single-letter designator needs a number and may occur once. `T` needs a `P` or a component before it, and a component after it. `(` cannot open a second group inside a skipped `(...)`.

Unaffected: unit names without numbers (`"day day"`), repeated shorthand units, `"10DT10M"` (documented), mixed ISO and shorthand strings, `format()` round-trips, and `"P1H"` without `T`, which the interval docs use.

The second commit fixes two `interval()` examples that spanned 2.5 years instead of the 2.5 hours they intend. `"2008-05-11/P2H30M"` and `"08 05 11/P 2h 30m"` both ended on 2010-11-11. They now use `"PT2H30M"` and `"30min"`, and a test pins them.

**The last commit changes the meaning of an input lubridate's own documentation and tests used**, so it is separate and can be dropped. In an ISO period without `T`, an `H` or `S` designator now starts the time part, so a following `M` means minutes:

```r
lubridate::period("P2H30M")
#> before: "30m 0d 2H 0M 0S"   (2 hours and 30 months)
#> after:  "2H 30M 0S"
```

`M` before any time designator is still months, so `"P3M2H"` is 3 months 2 hours.

The branch also carries the roxygen2 8.1.0 regeneration commit from the signed-durations PR, unchanged. It is needed for the interval.Rd update.

title: Fix integer overflow when parsing large numbers in period/duration strings
description:
The period parser accumulates each number in an `int`. Values above 2147483647 overflow, which is undefined behaviour in C and wraps in practice:

```r
lubridate::as.duration("3000000000s")
#> [1] "-1294967296s (~-41.04 years)"
lubridate::as.duration(format(lubridate::dseconds(2222222222)))
#> [1] "-2072745074s (~-65.68 years)"   # format() gives "2222222222s (~70.42 years)"
```

Period numbers are now accumulated in a `double`, exact up to 2^53. `parse_int()` is unchanged for the date-time parser. Tests cover the INT_MAX boundary, values well above it, 2^53, fractional large values, and the `format()` round-trip.

title: Honour the sign of ISO 8601 and shorthand period/duration strings
description:
`period()`, `as.period()`, `duration()` and `as.duration()` silently drop a minus sign in character input:

```r
lubridate::as.duration("-PT30M")
#> [1] "1800s (~30 minutes)"   # expected -1800s
lubridate::period("PT-0.5H")
#> [1] "1800S"
```

ISO 8601-2 allows a sign before the `P` and on individual components. CDISC SDTM uses the leading form, for example `"-PT15M"`, for times before a reference, so clinical data currently parse with the wrong sign and no warning.

The C period parser now treats `-` or `+` as a sign when it directly precedes a digit, `.` or the ISO `P`:

- A sign before `P` applies to every component: `"-P1DT2H"` gives -1 day -2 hours.
- A sign on a component applies to that component only: `"P1DT-2H"` gives 1 day -2 hours.
- The two multiply: `"-PT-30M"` gives +30 minutes.

Any other dash is still a separator, so unsigned strings and `"1 day - 2 hours"` parse exactly as before. Tests pin this.

As a side effect, the `format()` output of negative periods and durations now parses back. Before this change, `as.duration("-1800s (~-30 minutes)")` and `period("-2d 0H 0M 0S")` came back positive. This extends the round-trip from #1005 to negative values. Shorthand strings such as `"-1 day"` also keep their sign now.

The first commit only regenerates the docs with roxygen2 8.1.0. I'm happy to drop it if you prefer to keep the RoxygenNote.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: Fix out-of-bounds read on an unclosed parenthesis in period strings
description:
The period parser skips `(...)` so that `format()` output of durations round-trips (#1005). When the closing `)` is missing, the skip loop stops at the string terminator and then steps past it, so the parser reads whatever memory follows the string. The result depends on the string length:

```r
lubridate::period("   1d (")
#> [1] NA   # expected "1d 0H 0M 0S"
```

The fix stops at the terminator. The new test covers 41 padded variants. Without the fix, about a quarter of the assertions fail (21 of 82), returning `NA`, or garbage such as an extra minute.

title: # Fix interval %/% and %% errors, NA in setdiff(), century leap years
description:
### Report the operator the user wrote for %/% and %% on an Interval

`%/%` for (Duration, Interval) and (Period, Interval) in R/ops-integer-division.r dispatches to `trunc_divide()`, which computes `trunc(e1 / e2)`. `/` for those signatures is a stop-only method in R/ops-division.r, so the error blames an operator the user never wrote:

```r
int <- interval(ymd("2020-01-01"), ymd("2020-02-15"))
ddays(10) %/% int
#> Error: Incompatible classes: <Duration> / <Interval>
```

`%%` for (Period, Interval) in R/ops-modulo.r goes through `modulo_period_by_period()`, which calls `%/%` and lands on the same message:

```r
months(3) %% int
#> Error: Incompatible classes: <Period> / <Interval>
```

### Treat NA entries as not discontinuous in setdiff()

`setdiff.Interval()` in R/intervals.r computes `makes2 <- !aligned & inside` and then runs `if (sum(makes2))`. Any `NA` in `x` or `y` turns `inside` into `NA`, and the `if()` fails:

```r
x <- interval(ymd(c(NA, "2020-02-01")), ymd(c(NA, "2020-04-10")))
y <- interval(ymd("2021-01-01"), ymd("2021-02-01"))
setdiff(x, y)
#> Error: argument is not interpretable as logical
```

### Use the calendar year for February lengths in .int_to_period()

`.int_to_period()` in R/coercion.r converts `end` to POSIXlt and passes `end$year` to `.days_in_month()` at two sites. POSIXlt stores years since 1900, and `.days_in_month()` (R/accessors-month.r) calls `leap_year()` on an absolute year, so February gets the wrong length in years where the two disagree. For 2000 it receives 100: `leap_year(100)` is `FALSE`, `leap_year(2000)` is `TRUE`. For 1900 it receives 0, which the rule counts as a leap year while 1900 is not.

```r
as.period(interval(ymd("2000-01-20"), ymd("2000-03-01")))
#> [1] "1m 9d 0H 0M 0S"    # February 2000 has 29 days; should be 10d
as.period(interval(ymd("1900-01-20"), ymd("1900-03-01")))
#> [1] "1m 10d 0H 0M 0S"   # February 1900 has 28 days; should be 9d
```

Found during my most recent [ry](https://github.com/sims1253/ry) audit.

title: `as_week_start()` crashes with an opaque error for non-scalar numeric `week_start`
description:
Found this during my most recent [ry](https://github.com/sims1253/ry) audit

## Summary

`as_week_start()` raises an opaque internal error (`'length = 2' in coercion to
'logical(1)'`) when passed a numeric `week_start` of length > 1, instead of a
clear validation message. The bug is reachable from the public API through the
`week_start` argument of `update()`, `wday()`, and the round/floor/ceiling
accessors.

## Reprex

```r
library(lubridate)

## Direct internal path
as_week_start(c(1, 2))
#> Error: 'length = 2' in coercion to 'logical(1)'

## Public API paths
wday(as.Date("2020-01-01"), week_start = c(1, 2))
#> Error: 'length = 2' in coercion to 'logical(1)'

update(as.Date("2020-01-01"), wdays = 3, week_start = c(1, 2))
#> Error: 'length = 2' in coercion to 'logical(1)'
```

## Root cause

In `R/update.r`, `as_week_start()` checks the numeric range with a scalar `||`
before any length-1 check, and the length-1 guard lives only in the non-numeric
branch:

```r
as_week_start <- function(x) {
  if (is.numeric(x)) {
    if (x > 7 || x < 1) {                 # <- scalar || on unguarded x
      stop("Invalid 'week_start' argument; must be between 1 and 7")
    }
    return(x)
  }

  if (length(x) != 1L)                    # <- guard only in non-numeric branch
    stop("Invalid `week_start` argument; must be of length 1")
  ...
}
```

A length > 1 numeric `x` makes `x > 7 || x < 1` evaluate to a length-2 logical,
which the scalar `||` cannot coerce, producing the opaque error.

title: Implement `leap_year()` in C
description:
I noticed the [fastymd](https://cran.r-project.org/package=fastymd) package hitting CRAN recently. One of its features is fast leap year calculations, which made me wonder how lubridate stacks up.

Currently `leap_year()` is pure R and is relatively speaking quite slow. With the lubridate main branch:

``` r
library(microbenchmark)

set.seed(42)
years <- sample(4000, 1e4, replace = TRUE)

microbenchmark(
  fastymd::is_leap(years),
  lubridate::leap_year(years),
  times = 1e4
)
#> Unit: microseconds
#>                         expr   min    lq       mean median     uq      max neval cld
#>      fastymd::is_leap(years)  29.4  47.8   65.64309   52.6   64.2  11538.7 10000  a 
#>  lubridate::leap_year(years) 792.3 986.5 1203.30433 1020.2 1139.0 298644.7 10000   b
```

<sup>Created on 2025-05-01 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

This PR moves the leap year calculation to C, simply wrapping the `IS_LEAP` macro already used elsewhere in the codebase. With it I see a roughly 30-fold performance increase on my machine:

``` r
library(microbenchmark)

set.seed(42)
years <- sample(4000, 1e4, replace = TRUE)

microbenchmark(
  fastymd::is_leap(years),
  lubridate::leap_year(years),
  times = 1e4
)
#> Unit: microseconds
#>                         expr  min   lq     mean median   uq    max neval cld
#>      fastymd::is_leap(years) 29.2 44.1 64.90436   48.4 55.8  20797 10000   a
#>  lubridate::leap_year(years) 15.6 30.4 72.39227   34.6 40.2 310873 10000   a
```

title: Recycle all POSIXlt fields when doing period month/year addition
description:
Part of https://github.com/tidyverse/lubridate/issues/1069, specifically my comment in https://github.com/tidyverse/lubridate/issues/1069#issuecomment-1268892740

So now we get this in the current state of R-devel again

``` r
as.Date("2019-01-30") + months(0:3)
#> [1] "2019-01-30" NA           "2019-03-30" "2019-04-30"
```

I've checked that this fixes slider too.

I'm convinced that this was an R-devel bug and I've sent them a message here about it https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-devel/2022-October/082066.html. Nevertheless, I feel like we could be more robust about recycling the fields of the POSIXlt objects where possible to avoid these issues altogether. Relying on base R's hidden recycling of the POSIXlt fields seems dangerous, and I'm not sure it is really documented well.

We also actually use base R recycling rules (accidentally?) here due to the `+` call. I've opened https://github.com/tidyverse/lubridate/issues/1070 to track a move towards tidyverse recycling rules, but for now I have tried to keep the base R recycling rules intact.

This patch doesn't actually fix the `floor_date()` issue in #1069. But it is possible the fixing of the r-devel bug itself will fix that issue. I am not sure yet, but will look at that in another PR. It probably implies we are partially recycling POSIXlt objects somewhere else, so it would be good to track it down either way.

description:
Raising a small issue with `guess_formats()` along with a proposed easy fix.

Documentation of `guess_formats()` indicated that b & B are considered equivalent.  This is true in the actual parser called by `.strptime`, but not in the guessing code.  Previously, this could lead to parsing failure when "B" was used alongside data that only contained abbreviated months.  

A simple change in string substitution in the function appears to correct things issue.  Given the if-statement on the line just above the one edited, I think this is just fixing a typo to match what was already intended.

**Currently:**
``` r
require(lubridate, quietly = TRUE, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

# Data from examples of guess_format():

# A mix of full and abbreviated months:
mixed <- c("jan 3 2010", "January 5 1999")
# Just abbreviations:
abbrev <- c("jan 3 2010", "Jan 1, 1999")


# when using guess_format(), only the 'b' version matches both:
guess_formats(mixed, c("BdY"), print_matches = TRUE)
#>                       BdY        BdY       
#> [1,] "jan 3 2010"     ""         ""        
#> [2,] "January 5 1999" "%B %d %Y" "%B %d %Y"
#>        BdY        BdY 
#> "%B %d %Y" "%B %d %Y"

guess_formats(mixed, c("bdy"), print_matches = TRUE)
#>                       Obdy        bdy       
#> [1,] "jan 3 2010"     "%Ob %d %Y" "%b %d %Y"
#> [2,] "January 5 1999" "%Ob %d %Y" "%B %d %Y"
#>        Obdy        Obdy         bdy         bdy 
#> "%Ob %d %Y" "%Ob %d %Y"  "%b %d %Y"  "%B %d %Y"

# B thus offers no options with only abbreviated months:
guess_formats(abbrev, c("BdY"), print_matches = TRUE)
#>                    BdY BdY
#> [1,] "jan 3 2010"  ""  "" 
#> [2,] "Jan 1, 1999" ""  ""
#> NULL


# When dataset contains a mix of abbreviated & full names, 
# trained parsing works fine with either b or B:

parse_date_time(mixed, "bdy")
#> [1] "2010-01-03 UTC" "1999-01-05 UTC"
parse_date_time(mixed, "Bdy")
#> [1] "2010-01-03 UTC" "1999-01-05 UTC"

# But only b works if it's just abbreviations:

parse_date_time(abbrev, "bdy")
#> [1] "2010-01-03 UTC" "1999-01-01 UTC"
parse_date_time(abbrev, "Bdy")
#> Warning: All formats failed to parse. No formats found.
#> [1] NA NA
```

<sup>Created on 2021-05-15 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.0)</sup>

**With proposed change:**
``` r
require(lubridate, quietly = TRUE, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

mixed <- c("jan 3 2010", "January 5 1999")
abbrev <- c("jan 3 2010", "Jan 1, 1999")

# Both approaches now introduce 0b as option:

guess_formats(mixed, c("BdY"), print_matches = TRUE)
#>                       ObdY        BdY       
#> [1,] "jan 3 2010"     "%Ob %d %Y" ""        
#> [2,] "January 5 1999" "%Ob %d %Y" "%B %d %Y"
#>        ObdY        ObdY         BdY 
#> "%Ob %d %Y" "%Ob %d %Y"  "%B %d %Y"

guess_formats(mixed, c("bdY"), print_matches = TRUE)
#>                       ObdY        bdY       
#> [1,] "jan 3 2010"     "%Ob %d %Y" "%b %d %Y"
#> [2,] "January 5 1999" "%Ob %d %Y" "%B %d %Y"
#>        ObdY        ObdY         bdY         bdY 
#> "%Ob %d %Y" "%Ob %d %Y"  "%b %d %Y"  "%B %d %Y"

# And both work now fine with just abbreviations:

parse_date_time(abbrev, "bdy")
#> [1] "2010-01-03 UTC" "1999-01-01 UTC"

parse_date_time(abbrev, "Bdy")
#> [1] "2010-01-03 UTC" "1999-01-01 UTC"
```

title: Add vctrs support to lubridate
description:
Closes #721 
Fixes @batpigandme's comment in https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/issues/919#issuecomment-600680606

This PR adds vctrs support for Period / Duration / Interval S4 classes. Specifically, each one now has methods for `vec_ptype2()`, `vec_cast()`, `vec_proxy()`, `vec_restore()`, `vec_proxy_compare()`, and `vec_proxy_equal()`.

I have added an extensive test suite, testing the cast/ptype behavior, and also the behavior of various vctrs functions (ordering, binding, c, etc). I think these vctrs functionality tests are good because this is one way to ensure that your `vec_restore()` and `vec_proxy()` methods are right.

- There is no common type between Period / Duration / Interval. This could be added later if required, but for now this seems safe and should solve 95% of the problems.

- Duration and difftime have a common type.

- I have not prevented inheritance here (like we did in glue), as we expect inheritance in the cast/ptype2 methods to be prevented natively in vctrs in the near future.

- Period and Interval types use a data frame as their proxy, with a special optional `rcrd_names` column to hold any vector names. This is better than adding row names, because it allows duplicates. The comparison/equality proxies do not have this column.

- Interval types have a time zone attached. I followed the same rules as POSIXct when determining the common type.

   - Local time zones are overruled by the other time zone
   - Otherwise the time zone used in the common type comes from the LHS

- You'll see a `TODO` in the constructor section. Lubridate constructors are rather slow, and I'd really like to store a global empty `Period` and `Duration` object, but I can't seem to create one in the `.onLoad()`. If I call `period()` in `.onLoad()`, for some reason the S4 `initialize()` method gets bypassed, but the validity method still gets run and we get an error from there. I'm curious if anyone has ever seen this.

- This currently requires dev vctrs, but it is in Suggests.

- There was also a small bug where `interval(tzone = "my-tz")` wasn't respecting the `tzone` argument. This has been fixed.

title: Make round_date() really use week_start=
description:
After reading the documentation and many SO questions, I still couldn't really explain the difference between `round_date()` and `ceiling/floor_date` when using `unit="week"` and `week_start=1`.

I thought it might just be that `round_date()` ignore `week_start=`, a bit like `floor/ceiling_date` back in the #509 days.

Without `week_start=`, everything looks as expected. 

```
> date <- parse_date_time("November 27 2018 23:45", orders="bdyHM")
> date
[1] "2018-11-27 23:45:00 UTC"
> lubridate::round_date(date, "week")
[1] "2018-11-25 UTC"
> lubridate::floor_date(date, "week")
[1] "2018-11-25 UTC"
> lubridate::ceiling_date(date, "week")
[1] "2018-12-02 UTC"
```

But if you ask for weeks starting on Mondays (or any other day). Only `floor/ceiling_date` seem affected:

```
> lubridate::round_date(date, "week", week_start = 1)
[1] "2018-11-25 UTC"
> lubridate::floor_date(date, "week", week_start = 1)
[1] "2018-11-26 UTC"
> lubridate::ceiling_date(date, "week", week_start = 1)
[1] "2018-12-03 UTC"
```

Apart from this tiny glitch, thanks for the awesome library: I don't want to use anything else when it comes to dates 👍 !

title: [#407, #499] Import from methods
description:
# Motivation

This patch tries to resolve several cases where lubridate does not work reliably when methods is loaded but not attached. In previous discussions (#314, #407, #499, ...) the sense has been that this is R's fault rather than lubridate's. While I agree that having `Depends: methods` in the package description *ought to be* sufficient to ensure that methods is available, experience shows that it is not and I vigorously disagree that "make the user load methods for themselves" is a solution. See also the [R package guide](http://r-pkgs.had.co.nz/namespace.html#imports): "If your package is loaded, packages in Depends are loaded, but not attached, so you need to qualify function names with :: or specifically import them."

The current behavior leaves me, like previous reporters, in a bind because I want to use lubridate in my own packages without extending the cascade of `Depends`. The [general consensus](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/8637993/better-explanation-of-when-to-use-imports-depends) for what to do in this situation seems to be ["Contact the maintainer and ask them to do a more careful job of constructing their namespace."](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/14808337/tmplot-is-in-namespace-but-its-dependencies-are-not-found/14813080#comment20749830_14813080), so... hi, maintainers. Does it help that I come with a patch in hand?


# Contents

This PR follows the same approach as #314 -- it explicitly `@import`s the relevant functions (`initialize`, `coerce<-`) from `methods`. 

I gather that the two unresolved issues in #314 were [how to know what to import](https://github.com/tidyverse/lubridate/issues/314#issuecomment-101763989) and [how to test it effectively](https://github.com/tidyverse/lubridate/issues/314#issuecomment-101816694). I've punted on the first issue (I found `initialize` and `coerce<-` by tedious experimentation), but tried to improve the second one; the PR includes a set of tests which pass for me in all of `devtools::test`, `devtools::check`, `R CMD check --as-cran`, and on Travis.

title: Add shift parameter to quarters function when fiscal does not match calendar year
description:
A calendar year starts in January, but many places have fiscal years that start either before or after the calendar year. For example, a fiscal year might start in November, which means Q1 is Nov - Jan and Q4 is Aug - Oct.

The shift parameter causes two major changes, one is that the shift changes the quarter for a particular month, as described above. 2nd change is that it also increases the year by 1 if the quarter would 'normally' be Q4 but is now Q1 due to a shift. E.g. December 2015 is normally 2015.Q4 but would be reported as 2016.Q1 if the Fiscal Year started in December. 

Created new test cases as well, as I could not find any for the quarter accessor.

``` r
> naiss <- ymd_hms("1992-02-29 12:00:00")
> evt <- ymd_hms("2014-03-01 01:00:00")

[1] 21.99874
```

``` r
> time_length(interval(naiss, evt), "years")
[1] 22.00011
```

title: support for ISO-8601-formatted instants

Three functions are offered: `ymd_hms_z`, `ymd_hms_o`, and `helper_offset`.

`ymd_hms_z` is used to process strings like `"2012-03-04T05:06:07Z"`. It is a simple wrapper to `ymd_hms`; it passes the string to `ymd_hms` and sets the timezone to UTC.

`ymd_hms_o` is used to process strings like `"2012-03-04T05:06:07+00:00"`. It is also a wrapper to `ymd_hms`, but less simple; it parses the trailing offset, applies it to the instant, and sets the timezone to UTC.

Formatting output does not appear to be one of the purposes of lubridate, so I am trying very hard not to suggest feature creep. 

To format a date-time to appear as `"2012-03-04T05:06:07-05:00"` using the timezone of the instant does require a bit of effort, so the function `helper_offset`, is offered.

Also, some tests are included.   

There are doubtless better and more subtle ways to accomplish these goals. My only purpose is to suggest _a_ way.

title: Parser rewrite  (speedup of up to 200 times + heterogeneous formats)
description:
Hi,

I have rewritten the lubridate parser. It's not based on str_split anymore but on gsub, which has a massive speed improvement and comes close to the speed of `as.POSIXct`. 

I am often facing heterogeneous formats in a single vector, which is due to aggregation from different sources or just bad quality data which would have dates like "2011-12-31 12:59", "2010-01-01 12", "2010-01-01" in the same vector.  The new version of ymd and ydm_hms families can  handle heterogeneous formats. 

There is new low level function parseDateTime on which all other functions (including hms) are based. I have documented extensively all the parser functions and added examples to each of them. 

Here is the brief illustration of new functionality (lubridate:: prefixes hadley/master version):

``` R
> tt <- rep(as.character(Sys.time()), 10^5)
> system.time(out <- lubridate::ymd_hms(tt)) ## strsplit is not an option
Using date format %Y-%m-%d.
   user  system elapsed 
200.500   1.356 215.434 
> system.time(out <- ymd_hms(tt))
100000 parsed in %Y-%m-%d-%H-%M-%S order
   user  system elapsed 
  1.152   0.000   1.164

> tt <- rep("3:3:3", 10^5)
> system.time(out <- lubridate:::hms(tt))
   user  system elapsed 
 88.902   0.632  93.983 
> system.time(out <- hms(tt))
   user  system elapsed 
  1.296   0.024   1.382

```

Comes close to as.POSIXct:

``` R
> tt <- rep(as.character(Sys.time()), 10^6)
> system.time(out <- as.POSIXct(tt, tz = "UTC"))
   user  system elapsed 
 11.173   0.232  11.685
> system.time(out <- ymd_hms(tt))
1000000 parsed in %Y-%m-%d-%H-%M-%S order
   user  system elapsed 
 11.576   0.152  12.479
```

Heterogeneous formats:

``` R


> x <- c(20100101120101, "2009-01-02 12-01-02", "2009.01.03 12:01:03", "2009-1-4 12-1-4",
+        "2009-1, 5 12:1, 5", "2009....1--6 - 12::1:6", "20090107 120107", "200901-08 1201-8",
+        "10-01-09 12:01:09", "10-01-10 10:01:10 AM", "10-01-11 10:01:11 PM")
> ymd_hms(x)
1 parsed in %y-%m-%d-%H-%M-%S order
5 parsed in %Y-%m-%d-%H-%M-%S order
2 parsed in %y-%m-%d-%I-%M-%S-%p order
3 parsed in %Y%m%d%H%M%S order
 [1] "2010-01-01 12:01:01 UTC" "2009-01-02 12:01:02 UTC" "2009-01-03 12:01:03 UTC"
 [4] "2009-01-04 12:01:04 UTC" "2009-01-05 12:01:05 UTC" "2009-01-06 12:01:06 UTC"
 [7] "2009-01-07 12:01:07 UTC" "2009-01-08 12:01:08 UTC" "2010-01-09 12:01:09 UTC"
[10] "2010-01-10 10:01:10 UTC" "2010-01-11 22:01:11 UTC"
```

Truncated formats:

``` R

> x <- c("2011-12-31 12:59:59", "2010-01-01 12:11", "2010-01-01 12", "2010-01-01")
> ymd_hms(x, missing = 3)
1 parsed in %Y-%m-%d-%H-%M-%S order
1 parsed in %Y-%m-%d-%H-%M order
1 parsed in %Y-%m-%d-%H order
1 parsed in %Y-%m-%d order
[1] "2011-12-31 12:59:59 UTC" "2010-01-01 12:11:00 UTC" "2010-01-01 12:00:00 UTC"
[4] "2010-01-01 00:00:00 UTC"


> x <- c("2011-12-31 12:59", "2010-01-01 12", "2010-01-01")
> ymd_hm(x, missing = 2)
1 parsed in %Y-%m-%d-%H-%M order
1 parsed in %Y-%m-%d-%H order
1 parsed in %Y-%m-%d order
[1] "2011-12-31 12:59:00 UTC" "2010-01-01 12:00:00 UTC" "2010-01-01 00:00:00 UTC"

```

Fractional seconds. 

``` R

> options(digits.secs = 3)
> x <- c("2011-12-31 12:59:59.23", "2010-01-01 12:11:10")
> ymd_hms(x, frac = TRUE)
2 parsed in %Y-%m-%d-%H-%M-%OS order
[1] "2011-12-31 12:59:59.23 UTC" "2010-01-01 12:11:10.00 UTC"

> library(devtools)
> install_github("lubridate", "vitoshka")

> x <- c("2011-12-31 12:59:59.23", "2010-01-01 12:11:10")
> ymd_hms(x, frac = TRUE)
2 parsed in %Y-%m-%d-%H-%M-%OS order
[1] "2011-12-31 12:59:59.23 UTC" "2010-01-01 12:11:10.00 UTC"

> hms("3:3:3.34", frac = TRUE)
[1] 3 hours, 3 minutes and 3.34 seconds 
```

``` R
> ymd_hms("10-12-01 01:01:01 AM", "10-12-01 01:01:01 PM", 101010202020)
```
